title: 1xr631n
The Imams after Karbala: from Imam Zayn al-Abidin to Imam al-Mahdi
hook: How did a young imam who came out of Karbala alive begin a chain of guidance that moved forward through knowledge and patience?
scenes.0.text: When Husayn was martyred in Karbala, the leadership of the Imamate, or Ehl-i Beyt, passed to his sick son, Husayn. His real name was Ali. She was unable to attend because of her illness, and survived in the tent when her aunt, Zaynab, had her self-imposed a curfew. He returned to Medina with the rest of his family after travelling through Kufa and Damascus. Leadership, which was meant to be silenced by the sword, took on a new form in the hands of this young imam. Zayn al-Abidin carried his father's message to the nation not with a sword, but with tears, prayer and patience.
scenes.1.text: When he returned to Medina, he devoted his life to worship and prayer. She was also called Sajjad, because she bowed down a lot. His prayers were collected in the **Sahife-i Seccâdiyye**. The Shi'a call this book "Al-Muhammad's Psalms". He is also credited with the Rasool-ul-Hikmah, which describes man's rights to God, to himself and to others. He was poisoned and martyred around the 94th year of the Hijrah and was buried in Baku next to his uncle, **Hasan**.

scenes.2.text: Muhammad Bakr, son of Zayn al-Abidin, is known by the nickname Bakr. The name means "the one who penetrates knowledge". He established a great circle of lectures in Medina. And not only the friends of the Ahl al-Bayt gathered around him, but also scholars of different opinions. In this ring, besides his son, Kha'fer, there were also well-known names such as Katade, Zührî and Awzai. In the years of the heaviest of the Emirati repressions, the Prophet's knowledge was quietly but firmly disseminated. He was martyred by poisoning on the order of Emedi caliph Hisham b. Abdulmelik in 114 and was buried in Baku.
scenes.2.art.actors.0.label: uwc4s1
Imam Muhammad al-Baqir
scenes.3.text: His successor, Kha'fer-i Saddiq, lived during a turbulent period when the Umayyads fell and the Abbasids came to power. There were many rebellions around him, but Hadhrat Sadiq did not get involved in these rebellions and gave all his strength to science. The classroom in Medina became a large school where many students grew up. He taught in many fields, from jurisprudence to commentary to ethics. Today, the fiqh that Shiites follow is known as the Jafari fiqh. From how to take the abduction to who the imam was, many things were clarified by what he told us. He was martyred by poisoning in Medina in 148 CE on the orders of the Abbasid caliph **Mansur**.
scenes.3.art.actors.0.label: 1ytn1vq
Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq
scenes.4.text: The teachings of Ja'fer-i Sadiq were not only open to Shias. Abu Hanifa and **Malik**, founders of the Sunni sects, are among the beneficiaries. If it had not been for two years, he would have been destroyed. Nu'man is the proper name of Abu Hanifa, and this word describes the years he spent with Hadhrat Sadiq. And the Malik is said to have listened to him. His son, Musa al-Kazim, grew up in this ring with his father. The doors of the House were open to anyone seeking knowledge.

scenes.5.text: Muhammad was known in Medina for his knowledge, generosity and patience. A digger is someone who swallows anger. The Abbasid caliph Harounur-Rashid feared his influence over the people and had him brought from Medina to Baghdad. He spent the last four years of his life in dungeons and under strict surveillance. He was transferred from prison to prison, but he never lost his patience and devotion. He was martyred in Baghdad in 183 CE, in the prison of the Abbasid caliph Haroun Rashid, by poisoning on his orders. His tomb is today in Kazimierz, Baghdad, and attracts millions of visitors each year.

scenes.6.text: After the martyrdom of his father, Muhammad, Ali lived in Medina with knowledge and worship. The Abbasid caliph Ma'mun was alarmed by the successive rebellions of Ali's house. He wanted to make the love of the Ahl al-Bayt a shield to his throne. So he had Riza brought from Medina to the city of Merv in Khorasan. The Imam didn't want this trip, but they forced him to go. When the caravan reached Nishabur, thousands of scholars and students surrounded the camel's hooves. They asked him for a hadith. He recited Allah's words to the Prophet from his father, with a chain extending from there to Gabriel: "Laa ilaaha illallah is my pen. And whoever enters the fortress will be safe from My punishment". As the convoy progressed, he stuck his head out and added: "There are conditions. I'm one of them". This hadith is called Silsilet'z-Zeheb, or the golden chain, because the ravi'i are likened to golden rings. At Merv, Ma'mun first offered him the caliphate. He replied, "If this caliphate is your right, you cannot give the dress that Allah has given you to anyone else. You can't give me what's not yours if it's not yours". So he made Ma'mun his king. The imam resisted for two months. Finally, Ma'mun threatened him openly: "Either you accept the throne or I will cut your neck". He agreed on the condition that he would not interfere in the administration. He would not order, condemn, dismiss, or remove anyone. Then he said to his family, "Allah knows that I hate this. When it came down to accepting or being killed, I chose to accept". **Me'mun** gathered the leaders of different religions in the hope of testing the Imam's knowledge and embarrassing him. The chief bishop of the Christians, the religious leader of the Jews, the high priest of the Zoroastrians, and the scholars argued with Hazrat Riza. The Imam brought proof from the Torah to the people of the Torah and the Gospel to the people of the Gospel. None of them could stand up to him. Imran, a Sabaean, became a Muslim in that council. On a holiday morning, Me'mun asked for his holiday prayer to be recited by His Holiness. The Imam said, "I will leave as the Messenger of Allah left". He wrapped a white jacket over his head. Barefoot, with a staff in his hand, he went forth and brought back a token. Merv's streets filled with people crying. The commanders got off their horses and took off their boots. Wezir Fazl b. Sehal warned Ma'mun, "If the Imam arrives at the prayer in this condition, people will love him". Ma'mun immediately sent word and called the Imam back. He put on his shoes and went home. Me'mun saw that the Imam was no longer in his shadow. The Abbasids in Baghdad did not accept a successor from Ali's line and revolted. Ma'mun took Riza with him and set off for Baghdad. He knew what was coming to him. He said, "My father told me about his ancestors. I'll die before you, poisoned and oppressed. I'll be buried in a strange land, next to Haroun Rashid". So the caravan reached Tuts. One day, the Imam said to his relative Eba Salt al-Herevi: "I will go to this businessman tomorrow. Talk to me when I'm clear. Don't talk to me if I'm wearing a headscarf". The next morning, Ma'mun called him. There were plates of grapes in front of him. He embraced the Imam, kissed his forehead and handed him a bunch of grapes. He said, "Eat from this". He said, "Excuse me". He insisted, "You will eat. Or are you suspicious of us?" He ate three of my salsa. Then he dropped my scarf and stood up. He said, "Where?" The Imam replied, "Where you sent me". He came out with his head covered. He went into his house, closed the door and lay down on his bed. Sheikh Mufid also relates that Ma'mun gave him poisoned pomegranate juice with his own hand. Riza was martyred in the month of Safer in the year 203 of the Hijrah, in the village of Senabad, near Tûs, by poison given by the Abbasid caliph Ma'mun. Ma'mun seemed to weep and mourn. He performed his own funeral prayer and buried the Imam near the grave of his father Aaron. The village of Senâbad grew around the tomb of the Imam over time, becoming the city of Mashhad today. His tomb is today in the Iranian city of Mashhad. His sister, Fatima Masuma, had also gone to see her brother. He fell ill on the way and died in Qum, Iran. And therein is his grave. Mashhad and Qum are very important and sacred cities for Shiites.

scenes.7.text: Muhammad Taqi lost his father, Riza, at the age of seven, and the Imamate passed to him at that young age. The Abbasids took him to Baghdad and held him in custody. He was martyred there in the year 220 of the Hijrah, poisoned by order of the Abbasid c**aliph** **Mu'tasim**. His son, Ali Naqi, was brought to Samarra by the Abbasid caliph **Mutevekkil** and banned from leaving the city. He was martyred by poisoning on the orders of the Abbasid caliph **Mu'tez** in 254 AH. His son Hasan Askerli spent his entire life in Samarra, in a military camp. Military nickname means held in the camp. He was martyred by poisoning on the orders of the Abbasid caliph **Mu'temid** in 260 CE. Thus, all the imams from Hasan to Hasan Askery were poisoned and martyred, except for Hasan Ali and Husayn, who were martyred with the sword. The rulers of the time feared their knowledge and the love of the people. But they didn't dare to kill them openly with swords. Because a publicly shed imam could stir up a blood feud, stir up a revolt against the government. That's why each one was silently martyred with poison. The 12th Imam, the Mahdi, is still alive.

Imam Hasan al-Askari
scenes.8.text: Before the martyrdom of **Hasan Askeri**, a son was born in Samarra. This boy was the Twelfth Imam Mahdi. The Abbasids kept the imam's house under constant surveillance. Because of this pressure, the child's birth was kept secret. Hasan Askery was martyred in the 260th year of the Hijrah. Then the Mahdi went into hiding. The name of the first period is the little mystery. This is called the Unseen. The little mystery began in 260 and lasted for about seventy years, until 329. During these years, the Mahdi was hidden from the eyes of the people. But he didn't cut ties with the Shiites. Four special representatives mediated between him and the Shiites. These four are called Nuwab-e-Erbaa, or the four viceroys. In turn, Uthman b. Said al-Amri, son of Muhammad b. Uthman al-Amri, Husayn b. Ruhul-an-Navbahti and Ali b. Muhammad al-Samarri took over this task. The Shiites would give their questions and letters to these representatives. And the representatives would deliver the Imam's answers and letters to the public. In 329, the fourth viceroy Ali b. Muhammad al-Samarri's death was near. The Mahdi sent him one last letter. The letter said Samaritan would die in six days. After that, he was asked not to leave anyone behind. For the unseen had already begun, and it would not be revealed until Allah permitted it. The Samaritan died six days later. And so began the second period, the great mystery. It's called the Unseen. The great mystery continues today. During this period, the Mahdi has no personal representative. Shia seek advice from scholars who know the hadiths of the Ahl al-Bayt in religious matters. The Mahdi is not dead, he is hidden by Allah's permission. When God wills, He will come and fill the earth with injustice with justice.
scenes.9.text: **The Mahdi** is a descendant of the Prophet, the son of Fatimah. According to Shia belief, he was born and concealed by Allah's permission. In the end, when the earth is filled with oppression, he will appear and fill the earth with justice. Rumours about the Mahdi also appear in some Sunni sources. The Shiites wait patiently and hopefully for his arrival. That's called waiting. The last imam of the family whose water was cut off at Karbala will one day avenge the oppressed and bring justice to the earth. The chain of twelve imams, which began with Ali, is completed with him. May Allah hasten his coming. I'm going to be a good boy.
sunni.0.says: That Sunni scholars regard him as reliable in hadith and a mujtahid in jurisprudence; that Malik heard hadith from him; that he held scholarly debates with Abu Hanifa; that his death was in 148/765. The entry does not say "Abu Hanifa took lessons."
sunni.0.grade: SECONDARY (encyclopedia; the books of al-Dhahabi and Ibn Khallikan were not read directly)
sunni.1.says: The epithet al-Baqir, burial in al-Baqi', death in 114/733; that Sunni sources regard him as a reliable and conservative narrator; Qatada, al-Zuhri and al-Awza'i among his students.
sunni.1.grade: SECONDARY (TDV gives the year of death with "[?]")
sunni.2.says: His illness at Karbala, Shimr's attempt to kill him, and Umar b. Sa'd's obstruction; death 94/712 and burial in Baku; being Zuhri's main disciple.
sunni.3.says: Ma'mun's proclamation of him as crown prince in 817, the Imam's two-month resistance, death in Tus on 29 Safar 203 (5 September 818), Ma'mun's leading of the funeral prayer and his burial beside Harun, the name Mashhad. The bibliography has not been matched sentence by sentence.
sunni.4.says: Harun al-Rashid's taking him from Medina to Baghdad, about four years of surveillance and imprisonment, death in Rajab 183 (August 799); al-Tabari's history records it. The roles of Yahya al-Barmaki and Sindi b. Shahak are given as "reported."
sunni.5.says: Imam Muhammad al-Taqi: his marriage to Ma'mun's daughter Umm al-Fadl, death in Baghdad in 220/835; a note that the reports of poisoning are "not reliable." Imam Ali al-Naqi: al-Mutawakkil's bringing him to Samarra in 848, death in 254/868; poisoning is only a Shia claim.
sunni.6.says: That he was compelled to reside in Samarra and was not permitted to leave, death on 8 Rabi' al-Awwal 260 (1 January 874). The entry relies mainly on Shia sources and contains no Sunni source information.
sunni.7.says: The Mahdi narratives are not found in Malik, Buhari, Muslim; Ahmed b. Hanbel, Abu Dawood, in Tirmizi; a Sunni descendant of Hasan or Husayn in the latter days; Ibn Khaldun and Kādī Abd al-Jabbar's rejection.
sunni.8.says: The criticism that some scholars such as Ibn Taymiyya regard the Twelfth Imam as an imaginary person.
shia.0.says: Each imam's birth, knowledge, designation (nass) to the imamate, and death. Among the fundamental sources of Shia belief.
shia.1.says: Reports about the imams and the sections on designation (nass); also consulted for the birth and occultation of Imam al-Mahdi.
shia.2.says: The account of the minor occultation, the four deputies and the major occultation.
shia.3.says: The hadith of Nishabur and the "bi-shurûtihâ ve ene min shurûtihâ" appendix; the response to the offer of caliphate; acceptance of the succession under threat of death; predicting that the Imam would be poisoned; debate with the archbishop, Jewish leader, Zoroastrian priest and Imran es-Sabi.
shia.3.grade: Shiite primary source; text is at thaqalayn.net and lib.eshia.ir
shia.4.says: That Ma'mun first offered to relinquish the caliphate and, upon the Imam's refusal, proposed the crown princeship; that according to al-Mufid, Ma'mun's official was al-Juludi; that the Imam set conditions that did not legitimize the government.
shia.5.says: That after the death of Imam Hasan al-Askari the Imamis split into fourteen or fifteen sects; that the report of a son is the "official Imami view."
shia.6.says: The treatise on rights and duties attributed to Imam Zayn al-Abidin.
disputes.0.title: 102a68b
Were Abu Hanifa and Malik students of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq?
disputes.0.sunni: Malik's hearing hadith and scholarly conversations with Abu Hanifa are mentioned in both sources. In Sunni transmission this relationship is one of respect and meeting; the report of discipleship rests on secondary sources. TDV attributes al-Bukhari's not taking narrations from him in his Sahih to false words having been ascribed to his name.
disputes.0.shia: Malik's listening to hadiths and scientific discussions with Abu Hanifa are mentioned in both sources. In the Shi'a narrative, both of them used the knowledge ring of H. Ca'fer-i Sadiq; the word "those two years" is attributed to Abu Hanifa, an early source is not shown.
disputes.1.title: owww81
The deaths of the Imams: the poisoning report and the historical record
disputes.1.sunni: The years of the imams' deaths are recorded in history books. TDV does not find the poisoning reports for Imam Muhammad al-Taqi reliable; for Imam Ali al-Naqi and Imam Hasan al-Askari it relays this as a Shia report. In the case of Imam Musa al-Kazim, the Barmakid order is also mentioned as a report.
disputes.1.shia: The years of the imams' deaths are recorded in the history books. In Shia belief, all the imams except the Twelfth Imam were martyred by sword or poison; this narrative is based on the stories of Mufid and Kuleyn.
disputes.2.title: p8ckhg
Imam Ali al-Rida's crown princeship
disputes.2.sunni: That Ma'mun proclaimed him crown prince in 817 is reported by historians. The reaction of the Abbasid dynasty and the Baghdad uprising are also told within this period.
disputes.2.shia: That Ma'mun proclaimed him crown prince in 817 is reported by historians. In the Shia account the offer was accepted under pressure and limited by conditions that would not legitimize the government; the Imam did not desire the caliphate.
disputes.3.title: tztgu0
The Twelfth Imam and Imam al-Mahdi
disputes.3.sunni: Reports about al-Mahdi are also found in some Sunni books (Ahmad b. Hanbal, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi). The view of an imam who was born and went into concealment is not accepted; Ibn Taymiyya denies his existence, and Ibn Khaldun finds the reports weak.
disputes.3.shia: Reports about al-Mahdi are also found in some Sunni books. In Shia belief Imam al-Mahdi was born in 255 AH and entered occultation in 260; during the minor occultation there were four deputies, the major occultation begins after 329, and it is forbidden to fix a date for his return.
questions.0: Zayn al-Abidin survived from Karbala illness, and subsequent imams took up prayer with knowledge. Why do you think the imams continued to guide us in a difficult time through science and prayer?
questions.1: In the course of the teachings of Kha'fer-i-Saddik, the students of Ehl-i Beyt and the names of Katada and Zuhri are mentioned. Why do you think this shared science table is a sign of interfaith closeness?
questions.2: Musa Kazım and Ali Naqi lived under surveillance for many years. Why do you think they kept the circle of knowledge alive even under pressure?
questions.3: He accepted the succession after two months of resistance. Why do you think Ali Reza resisted first and then accepted?
questions.4: The narratives of the Mahdi are also found in some Sunni books, while the belief in the born and hidden Imam is unique to Shiite sources. Why do you think the difference between the sects is at this point?
summary: After Karbala, the imams, from Zayn al-Abidin to Hasan Askeri, often maintained the line of knowledge, prayer and patience under supervision. The mystery of the 12th Imam is the foundation of the Shi'a faith. The Mahdi narratives also appear in some Sunni sources.
key: The chain of the imamate after Karbala
notes.0: After Imam Husayn, the imamate passed to Imam Zayn al-Abidin.
notes.1: Imam Muhammad al-Baqir and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq founded a great circle of knowledge in Medina.
notes.2: Imam Musa al-Kazim, Imam Ali al-Rida, Imam Muhammad al-Taqi, Imam Ali al-Naqi and Imam Hasan al-Askari lived mostly under surveillance.
notes.3: The occultation of the Twelfth Imam, Imam al-Mahdi, forms the foundation of Shia belief.
notes.4: Reports about al-Mahdi are also found in some Sunni books (Ahmad b. Hanbal, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi). In Ja'fari belief the Twelfth Imam is Imam al-Mahdi, who was born and is in occultation.
sunni.9.says: It is said that the Twelfth Imam was born in 255 AD as the son of Hasan Askeri, and the Shiites considered him the expected Mahdi.
shia.7.says: The saying: "Speak when my head is open, do not speak when my head is covered"; the giving of a grape cluster by Ma'mun; the Imam's saying: "Forgive me from this", Ma'mun's insistence: "You will surely eat, do you have any doubts about us?"
shia.8.says: Acceptance of the succession on the terms "I will not command, I will not forbid, I will not give fatwa and judgment, I will not appoint and I will not abolish"; going out to the holiday prayer barefoot, with white yellow, bragging; Merv's crying, the commanders taking off their boots; Fazl b. Seal's warning and Ma'mun's recall of the Imam.
shia.9.says: Me'mun's threat, "If you accept the guardianship, no matter what, or I will strike your neck", and the Imam's statement, "I am left between acceptance and being killed".
shia.10.says: Fatima Mas'ume is the daughter of Musa Qasim and the sister of Riza; she fell ill and died in Qum in 201 while on her way to Iran to visit her brother and was buried there; her tomb is a major pilgrimage site for Shiites.
shia.11.says: The fourth deputy of the Mahdi, Ali b. Muhammad wrote to Samiri: "You will die in six days, do not leave anyone in your place, the unseen has begun, there is no manifestation without Allah's permission". Samiri died on the sixth day.
shia.11.grade: Shiite primary source; Tûsî text is at thaqalayn.net
